title: Acute pancreatitis
subtitle: Classify by organ failure, resuscitate moderately, delay intervention

sources.org: International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) and American Pancreatic Association (APA)

red_flags.text: Organ failure: hypotension, hypoxaemia, rising creatinine or falling urine output. Organ failure persisting beyond 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis and drives mortality.
Persistent systemic inflammatory response beyond 48 hours, which predicts a severe course.
Fever with jaundice or deranged liver tests: co-existing cholangitis needs urgent biliary drainage.
Rising intra-abdominal pressure with a tense abdomen, falling urine output and rising ventilatory pressures: abdominal compartment syndrome.
Clinical deterioration after the first week, especially new fever or new organ failure: suspect infected necrosis.
Sudden haemodynamic collapse or a falling haemoglobin: pseudoaneurysm bleed, which needs CT angiography and embolisation.

do_now.text: Confirm the diagnosis with two of three: typical pain, serum lipase or amylase above three times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging. Do not order an early CT just to stage it.

Start goal-directed intravenous fluid with a balanced crystalloid such as Ringer's lactate, at a moderate rate. Aggressive high-volume resuscitation caused more fluid overload without better outcomes.
Reassess fluid response frequently against heart rate, blood pressure, urine output and haematocrit or urea, and slow fluids once targets are met.
Adequate analgesia, oxygen to target saturations, and early referral to high dependency or critical care for organ failure or persistent SIRS.
Do not give prophylactic antibiotics for sterile pancreatitis, whatever the predicted severity.

assess.text: Aetiology: ultrasound for gallstones on admission, alcohol history, triglycerides, calcium, drugs, recent ERCP, and family history. Most cases in India and worldwide are biliary or alcohol-related.
Predict severity on admission and at 48 hours with a validated score; none is good enough alone, so repeat the assessment.

Classify by Revised Atlanta: mild has no organ failure and no complications; moderately severe has transient organ failure under 48 hours or local complications; severe has persistent organ failure over 48 hours.
Measure intra-abdominal pressure via the bladder in ventilated or deteriorating patients with a distended abdomen.

investigate.text: Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, glucose, triglycerides, CRP, arterial or venous gas with lactate. CRP above 150 mg/L at around 48 hours is a commonly used marker of severity.
Ultrasound abdomen on admission to look for gallstones and duct dilatation.
Contrast CT is for diagnostic uncertainty early, or for clinical deterioration or failure to improve, ideally at 72 to 96 hours after onset when necrosis is demonstrable.
MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound when common bile duct stones are suspected without cholangitis.
In deterioration after the first week, repeat contrast CT for necrosis, gas, collections, venous thrombosis and pseudoaneurysm.

resuscitate.text: Enteral nutrition is preferred to parenteral. Allow oral feeding early in mild disease; in severe disease use nasogastric or nasojejunal feeding.
Urgent ERCP within 24 hours for co-existing cholangitis. Early ERCP is not indicated in predicted severe biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis or persistent obstruction.
Abdominal compartment syndrome: treat medically first with decompression of the gut, drainage of ascites, sedation and fluid restriction; decompressive laparotomy is the last resort.
Suspected infected necrosis: start antibiotics that penetrate pancreatic necrosis, and delay any intervention where the patient allows.

definitive.text: Mild biliary pancreatitis: cholecystectomy during the same admission to prevent recurrence.
Biliary pancreatitis with peripancreatic collections: delay cholecystectomy until the collections resolve or for at least six weeks.
Infected necrosis: step-up approach. Percutaneous or endoscopic transluminal drainage first, then minimally invasive necrosectomy only if drainage fails.
Delay intervention for infected necrosis, ideally until the collection is walled off, around four weeks after onset.
Early open surgery is reserved for specific catastrophes: refractory abdominal compartment syndrome, bowel ischaemia or perforation, or bleeding that radiology cannot control.

escalate.text: Critical care for organ failure or persistent SIRS; do not wait for the 48-hour classification to ask for help.
Transfer severe acute pancreatitis and necrotising pancreatitis to a specialist pancreatic centre with interventional radiology, advanced endoscopy and HPB surgery.
Gastroenterology or advanced endoscopy for cholangitis and for transluminal drainage.
Interventional radiology immediately for suspected pseudoaneurysm bleeding.

notes: Severity is defined by organ failure and its duration, not by the amylase level. A very high amylase can be mild disease, and a modest one can be fatal.

In the first two weeks the enemy is organ failure and the treatment is medical. Early necrosectomy in sterile or early necrosis increases mortality; the surgeon's main contribution in this phase is restraint.
When a patient with necrosis deteriorates, ask three questions in order: is it infection, is it bleeding, is it compartment syndrome?
